summary: Nora can be asked what is on someone's Instagram story. The reading side is in place; it stays switched off until the bridge it reads through is deployed and the person index carries Instagram ids.
details: Asking about a story names a PERSON, not an account. Nora resolves who they are through the person index — the same file that already says who somebody is on Signal and WhatsApp — and will not work an Instagram handle out from a name: if she has not been told which account is theirs, she says so instead of guessing, because guessing wrong means reading a different person's story and saying nothing about it.
She only does this for people in a room she is in. Anyone else is refused, and she says that plainly — it is a boundary, not a failure, and she does not report it as one.

What comes back is a list of what is there — how many items, when each was posted, and a link each — never the pictures themselves. Looking at one is a second, deliberate step she takes only for the item that matters, so 'does Miles have a story up' stays a much cheaper question than 'what is in it'.

Stories are the only Instagram read that goes anywhere new. Profiles, someone's posts and search keep going where they already went; the story is here because the existing path has no way to read one at all. If a story cannot be read, she says she could not check — she never quietly answers a different question from a different source instead.
limitations: Not usable yet, in two independent ways, and both are visible as 'I couldn't check' rather than a wrong answer. The bridge the story read goes through is being built separately; and the person index has no place to record an Instagram id yet, which arrives with Instagram messaging.
X has no stories, so asking for one there says so rather than looking.
The whole capability is off by default and needs turning on deliberately, like every other feature that reads other people.

Nora keeps no memory of what she read — the pictures are not kept and the links expire on their own within hours. What she SAYS about a story in the room is ordinary conversation and lives as long as any of it does.
